newsitem.title: USA: Green groups sue Energy Dept over nuclear weapons.
newsitem.headline: Green groups sue Energy Dept over nuclear weapons.

text.p: Environmental and anti-nuclear groups sued the Energy Department on Wednesday to try to block its $40 billion programme to maintain and modernise the U.S. nuclear arsenal.

The lawsuit said the department failed to evaluate environmental effects of its programme to clean up and manage radioactive wastes from the weapons programme, and failed to explore alternatives to its costly, high-tech plan to keep weapons ready for use without violating testing bans.

About 40 groups including the Natural Resources Defence Council, Greenpeace and Peace Action asked the Federal District Court here to halt new construction for the weapons maintenance programme, which includes building a stadium-size laser facility and developing the fastest computer.

They said they feared that the weapons maintenance programme would drain resources from the 10-year programme to clean up contaminated sites across the country that were used to develop and build nuclear bombs.

"Given all the information, would taxpayers choose to fund pork-barrel nuclear weapons programmes or would they choose environmental programmes which protect future generations? This is precisely the analysis of alternatives DOE failed to carry out," Jay Coghlan, of a New Mexico group called Concerned Citizens for Nuclear Safety, said.
An Energy Department spokeswoman said the department would not comment on litigation.
The department has said that by using cutting-edge technology it could keep the nuclear arsenal safe and ready for use as a deterrent to other nations, without underground testing.

But critics said the programme would produce more radioactive waste and be a guide to other countries trying to develop nuclear weapons. They also said it mainly was a way to keep the Energy Department laboratories and weapons designers employed despite the reduced threat with the Cold War's end.

Tom Cochran, a senior scientist with the Natural Resources Defence Council, said the $4 billion per year, 10-year weapons stewardship programme allows new weapons to be developed, which undermines the purpose of the comprehensive treaty to ban nuclear testing.
